note: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin bought a maidservant, agreeing to pay in small copper coins. They did not have the coins with them, so they left a piece of silver as collateral. Later the maidservant's price went up, and the case came before Rabbi Ami. He ruled: there are no coins here and there is no silver here, so no sale has taken place.
why: Rav Naḥman has just ruled that a man who promises a hundred dinars for betrothal but hands over only collateral has given nothing; this purchase case shows the same principle, that collateral is not payment, applied to a sale.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage who rules that the purchase was never completed.

people.name: the sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
people.about: The buyers of the maidservant.

terms.meaning: Small copper coins; a peruta is the smallest coin of value.
An item handed over as security for a debt, which remains the debtor's property.

note: A man was selling strings of glass beads. A woman came and said: Give me one string. He asked: If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me? She answered: Give, give. Rav Ḥama ruled that any 'Give, give' means nothing, so she is not betrothed.
why: The Gemara is listing replies a woman might make when a man offers her something as betrothal, such as 'Give it to a dog' or 'to a poor person'. This opens a run of three similar cases about doubled words.

people.name: Rav Ḥama
people.about: The Sage who rules that 'Give, give' is not consent.

terms.meaning: Formally bound in the first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman an item of value that she accepts.

note: A man was drinking wine in a shop. A woman came in and said: Give me one cup. He asked: If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me? She answered: Pour me a drink, pour me a drink. Rav Ḥama ruled that any such reply means nothing, so she is not betrothed.
why: It follows the glass-bead seller as a second case of a woman's doubled words; the Gemara then asks what happens if she says the word only once, and rules that she is still not betrothed.

people.name: Rav Ḥama
people.about: The Sage who rules that her reply is not consent.

terms.meaning: Formally bound in the first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman an item of value that she accepts.

note: A man was picking dates from a palm tree. A woman came and said: Throw me two. He asked: If I throw them to you, will you be betrothed to me? She answered: Throw, throw. Rav Zevid ruled that any 'Throw, throw' means nothing, so she is not betrothed.
why: It is the third in a run of cases about a woman repeating a word when offered betrothal; right after it the Gemara asks whether saying 'Throw' just once is different, and rules that she is not betrothed either way.

people.name: Rav Zevid
people.about: The Sage who rules that 'Throw, throw' is not consent.

terms.meaning: Formally bound in the first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman an item of value that she accepts.

note: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone. Rav Ḥisda sat and estimated its worth: if it was worth a peruta she was betrothed, and if not she was not. The Gemara explains that Rav Ḥisda does not follow Shmuel here. The man's mother told Rav Ḥisda that on the day of the betrothal the stone was worth a peruta. He answered her: it is not in your power to forbid her to a later husband.
why: Shmuel has just ruled that an item worth less than a peruta here still makes a doubtful betrothal, since it may be worth more elsewhere. Rav Ḥisda's ruling goes against that, and the Gemara goes on to test it against witnesses in Idit who could say what the stone was worth.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: The Sage who values the stone and rejects the mother's claim.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling on low-value betrothal items Rav Ḥisda does not follow.

terms.meaning: The smallest coin of value; a betrothal gift must be worth at least this much.
Formally bound in the first stage of Jewish marriage; a betrothed woman may not marry anyone else.

note: A man betrothed a woman with a mat woven of myrtle branches. People told him it was not worth a peruta, so he said: Let her be betrothed with the four dinars wrapped inside it. She took the mat and said nothing. Rava ruled that silence after the money has already been given means nothing. Scholars in Pum Nahara challenged his proof, Rav Aḥai answered them, and Rav Aḥa bar Rav sent the question to Ravina. Ravina replied: We never heard that objection, but you who heard it should take the possible betrothal seriously.
why: The Gemara is gathering cases on when a woman's silence counts as agreeing to betrothal; the next case, a woman whose snatched belt is handed back to her, raises the same question.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that silence after the money is given is not consent.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage in whose name the scholars of Pum Nahara challenge Rava.

people.name: Rav Aḥai
people.about: Answers that challenge: not every woman knows the law.

people.name: Rav Aḥa bar Rav
people.about: Sends the question to Ravina.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Replies that those who heard the objection should be concerned about a betrothal.

terms.meaning: The smallest coin of value; a betrothal gift must be worth at least this much.
A teaching of the early Sages that was left out of the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

flag: The STORY runs from the myrtle-mat case (12b) into the Gemara's legal argument on 13a, starting mid-sentence; segments 5-7 are debate about a baraita rather than part of the story.

note: A woman was selling belts. A man came and snatched one from her. She said: Give it to me. He asked: If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me? She took it and said nothing. Rav Naḥman ruled that she can say: Yes, I took it, but what I took was my own.
why: It follows the debate on whether a woman's silence counts as consent. Rava then challenges Rav Naḥman with a teaching that a woman is betrothed with a coin snatched from her, and Rav Naḥman answers that there the couple had already arranged the marriage.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Rules that taking back her own belt in silence does not betroth her.

terms.meaning: Formally bound in the first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman an item of value that she accepts.

note: Rabbi Yehuda from India was a convert with no heirs. When he fell ill, Mar Zutra came to visit him and saw that he was getting much worse. Mar Zutra told Rabbi Yehuda's slave: Take off my shoes and carry them to my house, so that the slave's service would make him Mar Zutra's. The Gemara gives two views of the slave. Some say he was an adult: one man departed to death and the other to life. Others say he was a minor, and Mar Zutra did not follow Abba Shaul, who held that anyone may take a dead convert's minor slaves.
why: The Gemara has just said a master acquires a slave when the slave does labor for him, such as carrying him. Mar Zutra has the slave carry his shoes, an act of service, while the owner is still alive.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda from India
people.about: A convert with no heirs, who falls ill and is dying.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Visits him and has the slave carry his shoes so as to acquire him.

people.name: Abba Shaul
people.about: A Sage whose view on a dead convert's minor slaves Mar Zutra did not follow.

terms.meaning: A person who joined the Jewish people. A convert with no Jewish heirs leaves property that the first person to take it acquires.
A teaching of the early Sages that was left out of the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

note: The elders of Nezonya stopped coming to Rav Ḥisda's lectures, and he sent Rav Hamnuna to ostracize them. Rav Hamnuna asked them why they stayed away. They said Rav Ḥisda had not answered a question of theirs, so Rav Hamnuna invited them to ask him. They asked: if a master castrates his slave, does the slave go free, as he would for a visible injury? Rav Hamnuna did not know. They mocked his name: not Hamnuna, a hot fish, but Karnuna, a cold one. He went back to Rav Ḥisda, who told him the answer was in a teaching they could have cited, and began to quote it.
why: The Gemara is listing injuries that free a slave when his master causes them, like an eye or an extra finger. The elders' question adds castration, and the teaching Rav Ḥisda points to lists the body's extremities and, in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view, castration as well.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: A Sage whose lectures the elders of Nezonya stop attending.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: Sent by Rav Ḥisda to ostracize the elders; cannot answer their question.

people.name: the elders of Nezonya
people.about: Local scholars who stay away from Rav Ḥisda's lectures.

terms.meaning: To place someone under a ban that cuts them off from the community until they make amends.
A visible injury to a slave's body; a master who causes one must set the slave free.
A teaching from the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
In the laws of skin disease, a patch of healthy flesh inside a diseased spot that makes a person ritually impure.

note: Rabbi Elazar told of a Madonite in Jerusalem who owned a great deal of movable property and wanted to give it away. The Sages told him the only way was to transfer it along with a piece of land. So he bought a beit sela of land near Jerusalem and said: This northern part goes to so-and-so, and with it a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. Then he died, and the Sages carried out his words.
why: The Gemara is asking whether movable goods must be piled on the land to be acquired along with it. This case is brought as proof that they need not be, since a hundred sheep could not fit on so small a plot. The Gemara rejects the proof by reading 'sela' as rock-hard land, not a tiny one.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The Sage who tells the story.

people.name: the Madonite
people.about: A man in Jerusalem who gives away his goods through a small plot of land before he dies.

terms.meaning: Goods that can be moved, such as animals and barrels, as opposed to land.
A plot of land, apparently the size of a sela coin; the Gemara later reads it otherwise.

note: Rav Yehuda reported in Rav's name the case of a man in Jerusalem, sick by one account and healthy by another, who owned a great deal of movable property and wanted to give it away. The Sages told him the only way was to transfer it along with land. He bought a small plot near Jerusalem and said: This square handbreadth goes to so-and-so, and with it a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. Then he died, and the Sages carried out his words.
why: This is a second attempt to prove that goods need not be piled on the land to pass with it. The Gemara answers that the gift may have been money, which fits on a tiny plot, and then argues over why he could not have used another method.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports the case in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose account Rav Yehuda passes on.

terms.meaning: Goods that can be moved, such as animals and barrels, as opposed to land.
A measure of about the width of a hand, roughly 8 to 10 cm.
Two sides of an argument over how a dying person may give property away; the two accounts of the man's health match their two views.

note: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov sent his son Rav Ya'akov to study with Abaye. When the son came home, his father saw that his learning was not sharp, and said: I am better than you; you stay home and I will go. Abaye heard he was coming. A demon haunted Abaye's study hall, so dangerous that even two people entering by day were harmed. Abaye told the townspeople not to give Rav Aḥa lodging, since perhaps a miracle would happen. Rav Aḥa slept in the study hall, and the demon appeared to him as a serpent with seven heads. With every bow he made, one head fell off. The next day he told them: If no miracle had happened, you would have put me in danger.
why: A teaching of the Sages says that when father and son both want to study, the father comes first, unless the son is quick and sharp. This story is told as an example: the father judges his son not sharp enough and goes to study himself.

people.name: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov
people.about: A father who goes to study in place of his son and defeats the demon.

people.name: Rav Ya'akov
people.about: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov's son, sent to study with Abaye.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Head of the study hall, who arranges for Rav Aḥa to spend the night there.

terms.meaning: A harmful spirit; the Talmud treats demons as real dangers in certain places.

note: Rav Ḥisda kept praising Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man. Rav Huna asked that he be sent to him. When Rav Hamnuna arrived, Rav Huna saw that he wore no head cloth, as scholars did, and asked why. Rav Hamnuna said it was because he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and said: See that you do not see my face until you marry. Further sayings follow: someone says he would tell the Satan 'an arrow in your eye', and Rava tells Rabbi Natan bar Ami to marry off his son while he still has authority over him, between sixteen and twenty-two or eighteen and twenty-four.
why: The Gemara has just asked whether a man should study Torah first or marry first, and Shmuel ruled to marry first. Rav Huna's rebuke of the unmarried scholar shows that ruling put into practice.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Praises Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rebukes Rav Hamnuna for being unmarried.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A praised scholar who is not yet married.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Advises Rabbi Natan bar Ami to find his son a wife.

people.name: Rabbi Natan bar Ami
people.about: Receives Rava's advice about his son.

terms.meaning: Here, the evil inclination, the urge to sin.

flag: Segment 5 (30a) begins mid-statement with 'I would say to the Satan', a saying whose speaker and start are missing, and then moves to Rava's advice on when to marry off a son; it is not part of the Rav Hamnuna story.

note: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba came upon Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with a cheap covering thrown over his head, hurrying a child to the synagogue to study. He asked what all the rush was about. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answered with a verse: is it a small thing that 'make them known to your sons' stands next to 'the day you stood before the Lord your God at Horeb'? From then on Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba would not eat his morning meal until he had read with his child and added to his lessons. Rabba bar Rav Huna would not eat until he had brought his child to the study hall.
why: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi has just taught that whoever teaches his grandson Torah is credited as if he received it at Mount Sinai. Here he is seen acting on his own teaching, and it changes the habits of others.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: Questions Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's haste and then adopts the practice himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Rushes to bring a child to study, citing a verse.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Also would not eat before bringing his child to the study hall.

terms.meaning: Another name for Mount Sinai, where the Torah was given.
Here an idiom for eating the morning meal.

note: The Sages asked Rav Ulla how far one must go in honoring father and mother. He told them about Dama ben Netina, a gentile in Ashkelon. The Sages wanted to buy goods from him at a profit of six hundred thousand gold dinars, but the key was under his sleeping father's head, and he would not disturb him. In a second version, told by Rabbi Eliezer, the goods were precious stones for the High Priest's ephod, and Rav Kahana put the profit at eight hundred thousand. The next year God gave Dama his reward: a red heifer was born in his herd. When the Sages came for it, he said he knew they would pay any price, but he asked only the money he had lost by honoring his father.
why: Just before, Ulla taught that the nations accepted God's words once they heard 'Honor your father and your mother'. The question of how far that duty goes leads to this story, and afterward Rabbi Ḥanina argues that one who is commanded and obeys is greater than a gentile like Dama.

people.name: Rav Ulla
people.about: Asked how far honoring parents goes; tells of Dama ben Netina.

people.name: Dama ben Netina
people.about: A gentile in Ashkelon who gives up a great profit rather than wake his father.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Tells a second version of the story.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Teaches that the profit was eight hundred thousand.

people.name: the Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who rewards Dama with a red heifer.

terms.meaning: An embroidered garment worn by the High Priest, set with precious stones.
A rare all-red cow whose ashes were needed for ritual purification, making it extremely valuable.
A non-Jew, who is not commanded by the Torah to honor his parents.

note: Rav Dimi reported that once Dama ben Netina was wearing a cloak of gold and sitting among the nobles of Rome. His mother came, tore the cloak off him, struck him on the head and spat in his face, and he did not shame her.
why: The Gemara has been telling of Dama ben Netina as the model of honoring parents. After his honor of his father, this account shows how far he went in honoring his mother.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Brings this account of Dama ben Netina.

people.name: Dama ben Netina
people.about: A gentile whose patience with his mother is the model of honoring parents.

flag: Segment 5 ('and this action brings him to the life of the World-to-Come', 31b) is the end of Avimi's separate teaching about sons and fathers, not part of the Dama ben Netina story.

note: Rabbi Abbahu said that his son Avimi was one who truly kept the commandment of honoring parents. Avimi had five sons ordained as rabbis in his father's lifetime, yet whenever Rabbi Abbahu called at the gate, Avimi ran to open it himself, calling 'Yes, yes' until he got there. Once his father asked him for water, and by the time Avimi brought it he had dozed off. Avimi stood bent over him until he woke. This helped him, and he was able to expound the psalm 'A song of Asaph'.
why: Avimi has just taught that one son may feed his father pheasant and lose the World to Come while another sets him to grinding and earns it; his father now holds Avimi up as the son who honors properly.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Avimi's father, who praises him.

people.name: Avimi
people.about: Rabbi Abbahu's son, who serves his father with great care.

terms.meaning: Formally authorized as rabbis to give rulings in Jewish law.
The Torah's command 'Honor your father and your mother'.

note: Rabbi Tarfon treated his mother with remarkable devotion: whenever she wanted to climb into her bed, he bent down so she could step up on him, and whenever she got down, she stepped down onto him. He came to the study hall and praised himself for honoring his mother so thoroughly. The Sages there told him he had not reached even half the honor due to her, and asked him: has she ever thrown a purse into the sea in front of you, and you did not embarrass her?
why: The Gemara is collecting examples of how far the duty to honor parents goes, after Avimi stood over his sleeping father; this story shows that even extraordinary service can fall short of the full measure.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who served his mother by letting her step on him to get in and out of bed, and boasted of it in the study hall.

terms.meaning: A commandment of the Torah; here, the commandment to honor one's father and mother.

note: Rav Asi's elderly mother asked him for jewelry, and he made it for her. She asked for a husband, and he said he would look for one. When she asked for a husband as handsome as he was, he left her and went to the Land of Israel. Hearing that she was following him, he asked Rabbi Yohanan whether he could leave the Land to go meet his mother. Rabbi Yohanan said he did not know, and later said: Asi, you are determined to leave; may the Omnipresent return you in peace. Rabbi Elazar assured the worried Rav Asi that this was a blessing, not anger. Meanwhile Rav Asi heard that her coffin was coming, and said: Had I known, I would not have left.
why: Rabbi Yohanan has just said it is fortunate never to have seen one's parents, so hard is it to honor them properly; Rav Asi's story shows that strain, and the Gemara then turns to how one honors a parent in life and in death.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: A Sage whose elderly mother made demands he could not meet; he left for the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage Rav Asi asked whether he could leave the Land of Israel to meet his mother.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who told Rav Asi that Rabbi Yohanan's words were a blessing, not a sign of anger.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel. Leaving it for other lands was considered prohibited without a good reason.
A name for God, literally 'the Place', used in blessings and prayers.

note: At his son's wedding celebration, Rava himself served drinks to the guests. When he poured a cup for Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, they stood up before him. When he poured for Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda, they did not stand. Rava became angry and said: Are these rabbis real Sages, and those not Sages?
why: Rav Yosef and Rava have said that a teacher who waives the honor due to him has it waived. The Gemara raises this story as a challenge: Rava served his guests, yet was angry when Sages did not stand for him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who served drinks at his son's wedding and was angered when two guests did not stand for him.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A guest at the wedding who stood when Rava poured for him.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A guest who stood when Rava poured for him.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: A guest who did not stand for Rava.

people.name: Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda
people.about: A guest who did not stand for Rava.

note: At the wedding celebration of his son Abba Mar, Rav Pappa served drinks to the guests. When he poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, the guest did not stand up before him, and Rav Pappa became angry.
why: This is a second challenge, after Rava's wedding, to the view that a teacher can waive his honor. The Gemara answers that even when he waives it, others must still show him some act of reverence.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who served drinks at his son's wedding and was angered when a guest did not stand.

people.name: Abba Mar
people.about: Rav Pappa's son, whose wedding it was.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda
people.about: A guest who did not stand when Rav Pappa poured for him.

note: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok were reclining at the wedding feast of Rabban Gamliel's son, and Rabban Gamliel, the head of the Sanhedrin, stood and served them drinks. Rabbi Eliezer would not take the cup; Rabbi Yehoshua took it. Rabbi Eliezer protested: we sit while Rabban Gamliel stands and serves us? Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, a greater man, served his guests, who looked to him like ordinary Arabs, not angels. Rabbi Tzadok said: How long will you ignore God's honor? God makes the winds blow, brings the rain and sets a table for every creature; should not Rabban Gamliel serve us?
why: Rav Ashi has said that even if a rabbi may waive his honor, a Nasi may not. The Gemara cites this incident against him, since the Nasi served and the Sages accepted; afterward Rav Ashi's rule is restated as applying to a king.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, who served drinks at his son's wedding.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A guest who refused the cup from Rabban Gamliel.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A guest who accepted the cup and defended doing so by citing Abraham.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A guest who argued from God's care for every creature.

people.name: Abraham
people.about: The forefather, cited as a great man who stood over his guests and served them.

terms.meaning: The president of the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court, and leader of the Jewish community.
At formal meals guests ate leaning on couches; the host or servants stood and served them.

note: Bar Kappara (some say it was Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yosei) was sitting in a bathhouse when Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, came in and passed by, and he did not stand up for him. Rabbi Shimon was angry and went to complain to his father: I taught him two of the nine parts of Torat Kohanim, and he did not stand for me. His father answered: Perhaps he was sitting and thinking over what you taught him.
why: A teaching said one need not stand for an elder in a bathhouse. The Gemara cites this story as a challenge: the father excused the student only because he was lost in thought, implying one must stand even there.

people.name: Bar Kappara
people.about: The man sitting in the bathhouse who did not stand; some say it was Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Named in another version as the one who did not stand.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he had taught the man and was angry not to be honored.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Rabbi Shimon's father, who suggested the man had been lost in thought.

terms.meaning: An early collection of rabbinic interpretation of the book of Leviticus, divided into parts.

note: Abaye used to stand up as soon as he saw the ear of Rav Yosef's donkey coming toward him. Once Abaye was riding a donkey along the bank of the Sagya River, and Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis sitting on the other bank did not stand for him. Abaye said to them: Am I not your primary teacher? They answered: It did not enter our minds, which the translation takes to mean they had not seen him.
why: Abaye has just ruled that one stands for an ordinary elder only within four cubits, but for one's primary teacher as soon as he comes into view; both incidents show that rule in practice.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who stood for his teacher from afar and expected the same from his students.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage whose approaching donkey Abaye would stand for.

people.name: Rav Mesharshiyya
people.about: One of the rabbis on the far bank who did not stand for Abaye.

terms.meaning: The teacher from whom a person learned most of his Torah, owed greater honor than other Sages.

note: Ravina was sitting before Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti when a man passed in front of him without covering his head. Ravina said: How rude this man is. Rabbi Yirmeya answered: Perhaps he is from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are common.
why: The discussion is about the respect owed to Sages and teachers; Rabbi Yirmeya suggests that someone used to seeing rabbis every day may not show it, so the lapse need not be rudeness.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who called a passer-by rude for not covering his head.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
people.about: The Sage Ravina was sitting before, who defended the passer-by.

terms.meaning: A sign of respect; the man was expected to cover his head when passing a rabbi.

note: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan were traveling on a road and saw a man sowing different kinds of seeds together. One said to the other: Let the Master come and let us ostracize him. The other replied that he did not understand these laws. Then they saw a man sowing wheat and barley between grapevines, and again one wanted to ostracize him. The other answered that they follow Rabbi Yoshiya, who says a person is liable only if he sows wheat, barley and a grape seed in a single throw.
why: The Gemara has just said that the ban on sowing mixed seeds applies only in the Land of Israel, while grafting different trees is banned everywhere; this story shows Sages declining to punish a man for mixed sowing.

people.name: Rav Hanan
people.about: One of two Sages traveling together who came upon men sowing mixed seeds.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: His traveling companion.

people.name: Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: A Sage whose opinion on when mixed sowing makes one liable is cited.

terms.meaning: To place someone under a ban, cutting him off from the community as a punishment.
The Torah's prohibition on mixing species: sowing different seeds together, planting grain in a vineyard, grafting trees or crossbreeding animals.

note: One account of how Aher went astray: he saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator, who, as the translation explains, had been executed by the government, being dragged along by 'something else', a euphemism for a pig. Aher said: Shall a mouth that produced pearls lick the dust? And he went out and sinned.
why: Rav Yosef said Aher would not have sinned had he read the Torah's promise of reward as referring to the World-to-Come. The Gemara asks what made him sin and gives this as a second answer, after the boy who died doing a mitzva.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Literally 'Other', the name given to the Sage Elisha ben Avuya after he abandoned the Torah.

people.name: Hutzpit the disseminator
people.about: A Sage whose tongue Aher saw dragged in the dirt after his death.

terms.meaning: The speaker who repeated and explained a Sage's lecture aloud to the audience.

note: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. He said a formula and covered himself with boils and scabs; she performed an act of magic and he was healed. He fled and hid in a bathhouse so dangerous that even two people entering together by day would be harmed. The next day the Sages asked who had protected him. He said two of the emperor's guards had watched over him all night (angels, in the translation's reading). They said: Perhaps a forbidden sexual relationship came your way and you were saved from it, for a miracle is done for anyone who resists such a temptation.
why: Rava has just explained that one who 'sits and does not sin' is rewarded when a chance to sin comes to him and he resists it; this story illustrates such a person.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
people.about: A Sage who resisted a noblewoman's advances and was protected overnight in a dangerous bathhouse.

terms.meaning: Matronita, a Roman lady of rank; in these stories a powerful woman who tempts a Sage.

note: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok. He told her his heart was weak and he could not, and asked for something to eat. She said she had only non-kosher food. He said: What difference does it make? One who does this act may eat this food. She lit the oven to roast it, and he climbed in and sat in the oven. When she asked what this meant, he said: One who does that act falls into this fire. She said: Had I known it was so serious for you, I would not have caused you such anguish.
why: The Sages have just taught that a miracle is done for whoever escapes a forbidden sexual temptation, and cited a verse about 'mighty' people such as Rabbi Tzadok and his colleagues; this is the story that phrase refers to.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A Sage who escaped a noblewoman's advances by sitting in her lit oven.

terms.meaning: The place of punishment for the wicked after death, pictured as fire; the translation says this is the fire Rabbi Tzadok meant.

note: Rav Kahana sold baskets, and a noblewoman tried to seduce him. He told her he would go and make himself ready, then went up to the roof and threw himself down toward the ground. Elijah the prophet came and caught him, and said: You made me travel four hundred parasangs. Rav Kahana answered: What brought me to this, if not poverty? Elijah gave him a basket full of dinars.
why: It is the last in a series of stories about Sages who resisted seduction and were saved by a miracle, illustrating the teaching that whoever escapes a forbidden sexual temptation has a miracle done for him.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A poor Sage who sold baskets and threw himself from a roof to escape a noblewoman.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who caught Rav Kahana in midair and gave him money.

terms.meaning: A Persian measure of distance, a few miles; four hundred parasangs is a very long journey.
A coin; a basket full of them was a fortune.

note: A husband and wife disagreed over whom to marry their young daughter to: he wanted his relative, she wanted hers. She pressed him until he said: Let her be for your relative. But while they were eating and drinking at the meal, his relative came onto the roof and betrothed the girl to himself.
why: The Gemara is asking when a minor betrothed without her father's consent is still betrothed because he secretly wanted it. Abaye says this father kept his word to his wife; Rava says no one prepares a feast and then lets it go to waste.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, done by giving the woman (or a minor girl's father) money or an object of value; for a minor, it depends on her father's wish.

note: A man sold his property, stating that he meant to move to the Land of Israel. He went up but could not settle there. Rava ruled that whoever goes up intends to settle, and since he could not, the sale can be cancelled. Another version reports that Rava said the opposite: he meant to go up, and he went up, so the sale stands.
why: The Gemara has just argued that unspoken intentions do not count in a transaction. Here the seller stated his reason aloud, and the question becomes how far that stated purpose reaches.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the sale; two versions of his ruling are reported.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel; 'going up' is the usual way to speak of moving there.

note: A man sold his property intending to move to the Land of Israel, but in the end he did not go. Rav Ashi said: If he had wanted, he could have gone up, so the sale stands. Another version gives his words as a question: If he had wanted, could he not have gone up?
why: It follows the case of a seller who went but could not settle. The Gemara explains that the two versions of Rav Ashi's words differ over a man stopped on the way by circumstances beyond his control.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the sale; two versions of his words are reported.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel; 'going up' is the usual way to speak of moving there.

note: After Rabbi Meir died, Rabbi Yehuda told his students not to let Rabbi Meir's students in, calling them quarrelsome men who came not to learn but to overwhelm him with laws. Sumakhos, a student of Rabbi Meir, pushed his way in and reported Rabbi Meir's teaching that a priest who betroths a woman with his share of the offerings has not betrothed her. Rabbi Yehuda grew angry, repeated his warning, and objected that a woman is never in the Temple courtyard. Rabbi Yosei said: People will say Meir died, Yehuda grew angry and Yosei was silent; what will become of the Torah? He answered that a father can accept betrothal for his daughter there, a woman can send an agent, and she might push in.
why: The mishna rules that a priest cannot betroth a woman with his portion of the offerings; this teaching gives that ruling as Rabbi Meir taught it, and the Gemara goes on to the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who had died; his teaching is reported by his student.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who barred Rabbi Meir's students from his study hall.

people.name: Sumakhos
people.about: A student of Rabbi Meir who pushed his way in.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage present who answered Rabbi Yehuda's objection.

terms.meaning: The parts of sacrificed animals given to priests to eat. Some, of the most sacred order, could be eaten only inside the Temple courtyard.
To perform the first stage of marriage, usually by giving the woman money or an object of value.
The inner area of the Temple in Jerusalem where sacrifices were offered and the holiest portions eaten.

note: Shimon HaAmasoni (some say Nehemya HaAmasoni) used to draw a teaching from every 'et' in the Torah. When he reached the verse 'You shall fear et the Lord your God', he stopped, since, as the translation explains, nothing can be feared alongside God. His students asked: What will become of all the 'et's you have interpreted? He said: Just as I was rewarded for interpreting, I am rewarded for withdrawing. This stood until Rabbi Akiva came and taught that the 'et' in that verse includes Torah scholars.
why: The Gemara has just said that one Sage does not draw laws from the word 'et', and cites this teaching to show that this was a real method of reading that a Sage could give up.

people.name: Shimon HaAmasoni
people.about: A Sage who drew teachings from every 'et' in the Torah, then withdrew; some name him Nehemya HaAmasoni.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who later read the 'et' in 'You shall fear the Lord your God' as including Torah scholars.

terms.meaning: A small Hebrew word that marks the object of a verb and has no meaning of its own; some Sages read it as adding something extra to a verse.

note: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a plot of land when Rabbi Abba bought it. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, who said to wait for the Festival visit. Then he asked Rabbi Abba: If a poor man is reaching for a loaf and another takes it, what is he? Wicked, said Rabbi Abba. Then why did you do it? I did not know, he said. He refused to sell, since it was his first land and selling it was a bad omen, but offered it as a gift. Rav Giddel would not take a gift, citing 'he who hates gifts shall live', and Rabbi Abba would not use it because Rav Giddel had wanted it. Neither took it, and it was called the land of the Sages.
why: The Gemara has been telling of agents who bought for themselves what they were sent to get for another; this story extends the theme to someone who takes a deal another person is already pursuing.

people.name: Rav Giddel
people.about: A Sage negotiating for a plot of land when another bought it.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The Sage who bought the land without knowing Rav Giddel wanted it.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage Rav Giddel complained to.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak Nappaha
people.about: The Sage who confronted Rabbi Abba about the purchase.

terms.meaning: One of the three festivals (Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot) when people traveled to gather and hear the Sages' public lectures.

note: A blind man used to recite mishnayot before Mar Shmuel. One day he was late, and Mar Shmuel sent a messenger after him. The messenger went one way and the blind man arrived by another. When the messenger came back, he said that the blind man's wife had committed adultery. The blind man came to Mar Shmuel, who told him: If he is trusted by you, go and divorce her; if not, do not divorce her.
why: The Sages asked whether one witness is believed when he tells a husband his wife committed adultery and the husband is silent. Abaye says yes and cites this case; Rava reads Mar Shmuel as meaning trusted like two witnesses.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who advised the blind man after the messenger's report.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who holds one witness is believed and cites this case as proof.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who holds one witness is not enough in matters of forbidden relations.

terms.meaning: Plural of mishna: the short teachings of the early Sages, which students recited from memory before a teacher.
Jewish law usually requires two witnesses to establish a fact; the question is whether one is enough here.

note: King Yannai returned from conquering sixty cities in the desert and, in his joy, invited all the Sages to eat salty foods on tables of gold, in memory of their poor ancestors who ate such food while building the Temple. A scoffer, Elazar ben Po'ira, told him the Pharisees were secretly against him and urged him to make them stand before him while he wore the High Priest's frontplate. An elder, Yehuda ben Gedidya, then told Yannai to leave the priesthood to Aaron's descendants, since it was said his mother had been taken captive; the rumor was investigated and not confirmed, and the Sages were expelled in the king's rage. Elazar urged him to crush them, all the Sages were killed, and the world was desolate until Shimon ben Shatah restored the Torah.
why: Abaye holds that a single witness is believed about a wife's adultery and Rava disagrees. Abaye cites this account because the rumor about Yannai's mother was 'investigated and not found', which he reads as one witness believed unless two contradict him.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: A king who also serves as High Priest; he feasts with the Sages and then turns on them.

people.name: Elazar ben Po'ira
people.about: A scoffer, called evil-hearted and a scoundrel, who turns the king against the Sages.

people.name: Yehuda ben Gedidya
people.about: An elder who tells Yannai to give up the priesthood because of the rumor about his mother.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who comments that heresy entered Yannai at that moment.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: Restores the Torah after the Sages are killed.

terms.meaning: The gold plate engraved with God's name that the High Priest wore on his forehead.
Here, another name for the Sages.
The teachings handed down by the Sages alongside the written Bible. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak notes that, unlike a scroll in the corner, it cannot survive without them.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishnah, the core collection of Jewish law.

note: A man from Neharde'a, told at a butcher shop in Pumbedita to wait until Rav Yehuda's servant had been served, mocked Rav Yehuda with an insulting nickname. Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and, told that the man habitually called people slaves, proclaimed that he himself was a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Nahman's court, and Rav Huna advised him to go out of respect for the Exilarch's house. At Rav Nahman's home Rav Yehuda corrected nearly everything his host said: his words for a fence, a bench, a citron and a cup, his offer to have his daughter Donag pour drinks, and his offer to send greetings to his wife Yalta. Yalta sent word to Rav Nahman to finish with him. How the case itself ended is not told here.
why: The Gemara has just quoted the teaching that whoever calls others flawed in lineage is himself flawed, with Shmuel's comment; this man, who called people slaves, is the case where Rav Yehuda acted on it.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Yehezkel
people.about: A Sage in Pumbedita whose servant is served first; he excommunicates the man and declares him a slave.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A judge in Neharde'a before whom the man summons Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Advises Rav Yehuda to answer the summons.

people.name: Donag
people.about: Rav Nahman's daughter, a minor.

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Nahman's wife, who tells him to end the exchange.

terms.meaning: To put a person under a formal ban that cuts him off from the community.
The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia. Rav Nahman was linked to his household, so ignoring Rav Nahman's summons would slight it.
Saying a man descends from non-Jewish slaves, which meant he could not marry a Jew of unflawed lineage.

flag: The story stops before the hearing: Rav Nahman's questioning and its outcome begin in the following segments, which appear as a separate story (0D736B).

note: Rav Yehuda has come to Rav Nahman's court in Neharde'a, summoned by a man he excommunicated and declared a slave. He explained that the man had insulted a Sage's agent and habitually called people slaves. The man arrived, protesting that he came from the Hasmonean kings; Rav Yehuda quoted Shmuel that anyone who says so is a slave. When Rav Nahman objected to a ruling quoted after the fact, Rav Mattana, arriving that day after thirteen years away, confirmed it: the last Hasmonean girl had cried this from a roof, then fell and died. The man was proclaimed a slave and several marriage contracts were torn up. Townspeople chased Rav Yehuda to stone him; he threatened to reveal Shmuel's list of flawed families, and they threw down the stones, which dammed the Malka River.
why: The Gemara is listing families of flawed lineage; in this hearing Rav Nahman presses whether Shmuel's teaching lets one only suspect a man who calls others slaves, or also proclaim him one.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage from Pumbedita, summoned to court for declaring a man a slave.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge in Neharde'a who hears the case.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: A Sage, back in Neharde'a after thirteen years, who confirms what Shmuel said.

terms.meaning: A royal family of priests. In Shmuel's teaching, none of them survived except slaves and one girl, so a claim to descend from them marks a man as a slave.
The document a husband gives his wife at marriage (ketubah). Tearing them up meant those marriages were treated as invalid.
To put a person under a formal ban that cuts him off from the community.

flag: The story begins mid-scene: the insult, the summons and the dinner exchange that lead into it are in the preceding segments (story 4AB242).

note: In Rabbi Pinehas's day, people wanted to declare the lineage of Babylonian families doubtful compared to the Land of Israel's. Rabbi Pinehas told his servants that once he had made two statements in the house of study, they should pick him up on a stretcher and run. He first announced that slaughtering a bird is not required by Torah law, and while the scholars were absorbed in that, he declared that the Land of Israel's lineage is muddled compared to Babylonia's. His servants carried him off, and his pursuers could not catch him. The scholars then examined families' lineage until they reached ones too dangerous to accuse, and stopped.
why: The Gemara has just quoted the teaching that Babylonian lineage is purer than the Land of Israel's, and told how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi resisted the opposite claim; this is a second attempt at that claim, met the same way.

people.name: Rabbi Pinehas
people.about: A Sage who declares the Land of Israel's lineage muddled compared to Babylonia's, then has himself carried away.

terms.meaning: Family descent. A flaw in it, such as descent from a forbidden union, could bar a person from marrying into other families.
Mixed with families of doubtful descent, so that marrying into them would require checking first.
The hall where the Sages and their students met to learn and debate.

note: Ze'eiri, a Babylonian Sage, kept avoiding Rabbi Yohanan of the Land of Israel, who kept asking him to marry his daughter. One day on the road, Ze'eiri lifted Rabbi Yohanan onto his shoulders and carried him across a large puddle. Rabbi Yohanan said: our Torah is fit in your eyes, but our daughters are not? He argued that if Ze'eiri feared the flawed families who had come up from Babylonia, some must have stayed behind in Babylonia too. The Gemara comments that Rabbi Yohanan had missed Rabbi Elazar's teaching that Ezra left Babylonia only after making it pure like fine flour. Ze'eiri's reply is not given.
why: The Gemara has just said that anyone who speaks like a Babylonian may marry without having his lineage checked, since Babylonian families are presumed unflawed; here a Babylonian Sage holds back from marrying into a family of the Land of Israel.

people.name: Ze'eiri
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who avoids marrying Rabbi Yohanan's daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel who keeps offering his daughter to Ze'eiri.

terms.meaning: A passage of the Mishnah, the core early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses.
A mishna lists ten classes of Jews by descent who came up from Babylonia with Ezra, from priests and Levites down to those of flawed lineage.

note: Ulla visited Rav Yehuda in Pumbedita and saw that his son, Rav Yitzhak, was grown but unmarried. Asked why, Rav Yehuda said he did not know where he could find a wife for him. Ulla answered that none of them could be sure of their own descent: they might come from the women ravished in Zion, or from the people the prophet Amos describes lying on ivory beds, whom Rabbi Abbahu explains as men who swapped wives. When Rav Yehuda asked what to do, Ulla told him to go by silence, as the people of the Land of Israel do: when two people quarrel, the one who falls silent first is of finer lineage.
why: The Gemara is discussing how to know which families have unflawed lineage; Ulla's advice gives a practical test, which Rav then applies to Babylonia in the lines that follow.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visitor to Pumbedita who questions Rav Yehuda and advises him.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Ulla's host, who fears he cannot find a wife of sure lineage for his son.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak
people.about: Rav Yehuda's son, grown and still unmarried.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage whose reading of the verse in Amos Rabbi Abbahu ridicules.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage who offers a harsher reading of the verse in Amos.

terms.meaning: The Babylonian Sages' name for the Land of Israel.
Family descent. A flaw in it, such as descent from adultery, could bar a person from marrying into other families.

note: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the crowd pelted him with their etrogim. Rava said no one should teach such a thing where converts are common. Rava himself then taught there that a convert may marry a priest's daughter, and they carried him on silk. When he later taught them that a convert may marry a mamzeret, they told him he had spoiled his first teaching. Rava answered that he had done them good: a convert may marry from either group, as he wishes.
why: The Gemara has just cited support for Rav's view that priests' daughters may marry men barred from the priesthood, after debating whether converts may marry a mamzeret; Rava's two teachings state both rulings, which the Gemara then adopts as law.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who criticizes Rabbi Zeira and then teaches both rulings himself.

terms.meaning: A person born outside the Jewish people who has joined it.
A woman born of a forbidden union such as adultery or incest. She may not marry most Jews.
Citrons, the fruit held during the festival of Sukkot; the crowd evidently had them in hand.

note: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host, the son of a convert, quarreled with Rav Beivai over which of them would hold an official post in the city. They came before Rav Yosef, who cited the verse about appointing a king 'from among your brothers' to rule that every appointment must go to someone from among the Jewish people. Rav Adda bar Ahava asked whether that applies even when the mother was born Jewish; Rav Yosef said such a man counts as 'from among your brothers'. So Rav Beivai, a great scholar, would oversee the city's religious matters and the host its other affairs. Abaye remarked that whoever hosts a scholar should host one like Rav Adda bar Ahava, who knows how to argue in his favor.
why: The mishna says anyone whose ancestors held public posts may marry into the priesthood without checking, and the Gemara asks whether people of flawed lineage are ever appointed; this case shows who may hold a post.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage whose question wins his host the appointment.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: A great scholar who competes with the host for the post.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who decides between them.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who draws the moral about hosting scholars.

terms.meaning: A person born outside the Jewish people who has joined it. Here the host's father was a convert and his mother was born Jewish.

note: A woman came to Jerusalem carrying a child on her shoulders, and she raised him. He later had intercourse with her, and they were brought to court and stoned. The report, passed down in bar Kappara's name, stresses that it was not certain he was her son; he had clung to her, and that was enough.
why: Rabbi Yohanan holds that a court may flog, stone or burn on the basis of presumed status alone, without witnesses to the family tie; this incident is cited as a death sentence resting on such a presumption.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: The Sage in whose name the incident is reported.

terms.meaning: What everyone takes to be true from how people live, here that a boy who clung to a woman was her son.
Stoning was one of the death penalties a Jewish court could impose, here for intercourse between mother and son.

note: Captive women who had been brought to Neharde'a were lodged in the upper room of Rav Amram the Pious, and the ladder was taken away. When one of them passed the opening, it was as though a light shone through it. Rav Amram seized a ladder that ten men could not lift and began to climb. Halfway up he braced himself and cried out: Fire in the house of Amram! The Sages came and said he had shamed them; he answered that it was better to be shamed in this world than in the World-to-Come. He made his evil inclination leave him, and it came out like a pillar of fire. He told it: you are fire and I am flesh, and still I am stronger than you.
why: The Gemara has been discussing how to keep men and women from being alone together, with Abaye and Rava setting up barriers and Avin warning that festivals are the dangerous time; this story shows even a pious Sage nearly overcome.

people.name: Rav Amram the Pious
people.about: The Sage who hosts the captive women and overcomes his desire halfway up the ladder.

terms.meaning: Jewish women taken prisoner and then freed, usually by being ransomed.
The urge to do wrong, pictured here as a force that can be made to leave a person.
The life after this one, where people are judged for how they lived.

note: Rabbi Meir used to mock sinners. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman on the far side of a river. There was no ferry, so he took hold of a rope bridge and started across. Halfway over, it left him and said that if heaven were not proclaiming 'Be careful with Rabbi Meir and his Torah', it would have made his blood worth two ma'a.
why: The Gemara is discussing the pull of temptation between men and women; after Rav Amram's struggle it tells of Sages who scoffed at sinners and were shown how close they came to falling.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who mocked sinners until he was tempted himself.

people.name: Satan
people.about: Appears to Rabbi Meir as a woman across the river.

terms.meaning: A small coin. Blood worth two ma'a means a life made worthless.
Here the same as the evil inclination, the tempter who lures a person to sin; the story uses both names.

note: Rabbi Akiva also used to mock sinners. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree. He took hold of the tree and began to climb. Halfway up, it left him and said that if heaven were not proclaiming 'Be careful with Rabbi Akiva and his Torah', it would have made his blood worth two ma'a.
why: This is the second of a run of stories, after Rabbi Meir's, about Sages who scoffed at sinners and were shown how close they came to falling, in a discussion of the pull of temptation between men and women.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who mocked sinners until he was tempted himself.

people.name: Satan
people.about: Appears to Rabbi Akiva as a woman at the top of a palm tree.

terms.meaning: A small coin. Blood worth two ma'a means a life made worthless.
Here the same as the evil inclination, the tempter who lures a person to sin; the story uses both names.

note: The Sage Peleimu used to say every day: An arrow in Satan's eye. On the eve of Yom Kippur, Satan came to his door as a poor man. Peleimu gave him bread, then at his complaints brought him inside and seated him at the table, where he sat covered in boils and pus, behaving repulsively. Given a cup, he spat phlegm into it; when they scolded him, he collapsed and seemed to die, and people cried: Peleimu killed a man! Peleimu fled and hid in the bathroom. Satan followed and fell before him, and seeing him suffer, revealed himself. Asked what he should say instead, Peleimu was told: May the Merciful One rebuke Satan.
why: This follows the accounts of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Akiva, who mocked sinners and were tested; here a Sage who taunts Satan daily is taught to ask God to rebuke him instead.

people.name: Peleimu
people.about: A Sage who taunted Satan every day.

people.name: Satan
people.about: Comes to Peleimu disguised as a poor man and torments him.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, a fast day; the day before it is marked by a festive meal.
A name for God.

note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi prayed every time he fell on his face in prayer: May the Merciful One save us from the evil inclination. His wife heard and wondered why, since he had kept away from her for years. One day, while he studied in his garden, she adorned herself and walked back and forth past him, saying she was Haruta, returning from her day. He propositioned her; she asked for a pomegranate from the top of a tree, he brought it, and they had intercourse. At home, his wife was lighting the oven and he climbed in and sat inside it. When she said it had been her, he ignored her until she gave him signs. He said: I, in any case, intended to sin. All his days he fasted, until he died by that death.
why: Right after this, the Gemara shows from verses that one who meant to sin needs atonement even if no sin took place; Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi's lifelong fasting puts that idea into a life.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi
people.about: A Sage who prays to be saved from temptation and falls for his own disguised wife.

people.name: Haruta
people.about: The name his wife gives while disguised; the translation explains it as a prostitute's name.

terms.meaning: A posture of private prayer, bowing low with the face covered.
The urge to do wrong, especially sexual temptation in this story.

note: Rav Aha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and placed his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether he did not think she might already be betrothed. Rav Aha replied that if so, Rav Hisda had broken Rav's rule against betrothing a daughter while she is a minor, before she can say whom she wants. Rav Hisda countered that Rav Aha was breaking Shmuel's rule that one may not make use of a woman. Rav Aha answered that he followed another saying of Shmuel: everything is permitted when done for the sake of Heaven.
why: The Gemara is discussing how close a man may be to young relatives, and Rav Hisda has just ruled that a father may not sleep near a daughter once she is ashamed before him; this story shows where affection toward a granddaughter stands.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Abba
people.about: Rav Hisda's father-in-law, who holds his granddaughter on his lap.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The son-in-law he is visiting, who questions him.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, after which a woman is legally bound to her husband. A father could betroth his daughter while she was still a minor.
Being served or attended by a woman, which Shmuel forbade as too intimate.
Done with pure intentions, here out of family affection with no hint of desire.
